members: [Member 1] · adversary profile and attack lifecycle (slides 1 to 4)
[Member 2] · payload, RaaS structure, victims and negotiation (slides 5 to 8)

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Hi, we're presenting our investigation of the RansomHub ransomware campaign. I'm [Member 1], and I'll cover the adversary profile and the attack lifecycle. [Member 2] will then cover the payload, how the ransomware-as-a-service model worked, who it hit and how it negotiated. [Member 3] will finish with law enforcement and our recommendations. Each of us researched and wrote the sections we present.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: RansomHub appeared in February 2024 and had at least 210 victims within six months, according to the FBI and CISA. In the intrusion we modelled, the attacker went from guessing RDP passwords to encrypting the whole domain in about 118 hours. On 1 April 2025 the brand simply vanished, and no police agency claimed credit. Our main finding is that RansomHub was a brand wrapped around a mobile workforce of affiliates. For defenders, the leverage is in those six noisy days before encryption.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: We built our Diamond Model on one incident, documented by The DFIR Report, from November 2024. The adversary is an unnamed RansomHub affiliate. The attacker's remote-access tool logged a display name, johnattan, and a machine name, WINVM, and the clipboard showed a VirtualBox address, so they were working from a virtual machine. The capabilities were password spraying, Mimikatz, two commercial remote-management tools, Rclone and the RansomHub encryptor. The infrastructure was two spray addresses, one logon address and an exfiltration server on port 443. The victim's name and sector were withheld, so that vertex is the weakest, and we can't see the ransom negotiation either.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Here's the same incident as a timeline. Day one: the password spray succeeds, the attacker moves to the domain controllers and dumps credentials with DCSync. Day two: network scans, and the remote-management tool Atera goes onto the backup servers. Day three: Rclone copies 2.03 gigabytes out in about forty minutes. Day five: they come back through Splashtop and reset passwords. Day six: the encryptor spreads over SMB, stops virtual machines, deletes shadow copies, clears logs and encrypts. Every box at the bottom is a point where a defender could have stopped this before day six. I'll hand over to [Member 2] for the payload and the business model.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 2]. The payload does three jobs. First, it encrypts. Each victim gets its own Curve25519 key pair, and large files are only partly encrypted, one megabyte on and two skipped, which makes it fast. The ransom note has no price, just a link to a private chat. Second, it prevents recovery: it stops virtual machines and about thirty processes, deletes shadow copies, and clears the Windows event logs. Third, it protects itself. It won't run without a password, it spreads over SMB as randomly named services, and the operators built their own EDR killer, EDRKillShifter, which uses a vulnerable driver to switch off security tools.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Affiliates joined for the money. They kept ninety percent of every ransom and received it into their own wallets. That mattered because ALPHV had just kept a twenty-two million dollar payment from its own affiliate. The operators supplied the ransomware builds, the EDR killer, a chat panel and the leak site. The affiliates brought access, tools and their own servers. There were house rules too: no attacks on the former Soviet states, Cuba, North Korea or China, no re-attacking victims who paid, and only data extortion for non-profit hospitals. Those rules protect the brand, because victims only pay if they believe paying works.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: The FBI counted victims across eleven critical-infrastructure sectors, with manufacturing and healthcare leading, and the US, UK, Spain, France and Italy hit hardest. Public cases include Christie's, Frontier Communications, Kawasaki Motors Europe and the second extortion of Change Healthcare. Our assessment is that RansomHub didn't really pick sectors. Its victims were whoever had exposed RDP or an unpatched Citrix or Fortinet device, chosen independently by many affiliates. Where there was a choice, it leaned toward leverage, especially healthcare data, where a leak brings regulators.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Only one RansomHub chat appears among 295 public negotiation logs, because each victim got a private chat run by the affiliate. Incident-response firm Arete gives us the averages: a median opening demand of nine hundred thousand dollars against a median payment of three hundred and fifty thousand, so payers settled at about forty percent. The public cases show the pressure tactics. RansomHub claimed half a million Christie's clients; Christie's notified about forty-six thousand. It claimed two million Frontier customers; Frontier notified about seven hundred and fifty thousand. Kawasaki got a countdown clock, refused, and 487 gigabytes were published. Now over to [Member 3] for law enforcement.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 3]. Law enforcement ended up helping RansomHub. The FBI disrupted ALPHV in December 2023 and Operation Cronos hit LockBit in February 2024. RansomHub launched between the two and recruited their displaced affiliates. The joint CISA and FBI advisory in August 2024 published its tools and indicators, but tradecraft didn't change; our November case followed that advisory almost exactly. Charges against a Scattered Spider member, a documented RansomHub affiliate, came in September 2025, after RansomHub had already gone dark. No action ever touched the core operators. Our judgement, with moderate confidence, is that the pressure displaced RansomHub's affiliates, who moved on to DragonForce and Qilin.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: On Monday morning, a defender should start by detecting the long middle of the attack: password spraying followed by a successful RDP logon, DCSync from a machine that isn't a domain controller, Rclone or SFTP on port 443, and remote-management tools nobody approved. In a response, assume data was stolen before encryption, and check the attacker's data claims against your own logs, because RansomHub inflated them more than tenfold. To mitigate, take RDP off the internet, patch the edge CVEs CISA lists, and use tiered admin accounts. For resilience, keep offline backups with separate credentials, decide your payment policy before you need it, and track affiliates, not brands. Thank you.
